Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because the commander took his prize, Briseis. According to Homer's account, Achilles was angry that Agamemnon threatened to take away his prize—the reward he had earned through his efforts in battle—while Agamemnon's own prize remained far greater [1]. Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain dishonored and continue fighting to accumulate wealth for Agamemnon [1]. According to Apollodorus, Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of Chryses the priest [2].

Zeus married multiple figures across Greek mythology. According to Homer, Zeus married Hera [1]. Hesiod, however, describes Zeus as married to several goddesses: Themis, Mnemosyne, Leto, and Eurynome [2][3][4][5]. Apollodorus presents yet another account, stating that Zeus first married Metis [6], then Hera [7], and also had a union with Alcmena [8]. The Homeric Hymns add further variations, describing Zeus as married to Maia [9], Leda [10], and Demeter [11]. These conflicting accounts reflect the diverse mythological traditions preserved across different ancient sources.
